hiccup in Latin

hiccup

singultus, singultūs m. · singultiō, singultīre

Ancient LatinQuotationsComposed phrasesDraft
  • singultus, singultūs m. — a hiccup; hiccups; also a sob classical (Sen. Ep. 47.3: tussis, sternūmenta, singultus) Seneca lists the noises that slaves serving at dinner were beaten for, even involuntary ones: coughing, sneezing, hiccups.
  • singultiō, singultīre — have hiccups classical (Cels. 5.26; Plin. NH 23.48: singultientibus)
  • singultō, singultāre — hiccup; mostly of sobbing classical also used (Quint. 10.7.10: singultantium modō)
  • Singultīs? Bibe paulum aquae. — Hiccups? Drink a little water. composed
  • Anētum quoque ructūs movet … singultūs cohibet. — Dill also brings up wind … and stops hiccups: a herbal remedy. (Plin. NH 20.196)
  • singultūs sēdat — it settles hiccups (of another plant) (Plin. NH 21.120)

See also: burp, tickle, Herbal remedies.

Sources & evidence

Lewis & Short: singultus · Lewis & Short: singultio · Lewis & Short: singulto · Lewis & Short: anethum

Quotations checked against the Perseus Latin texts: Seneca’s letters, Celsus, and Pliny’s Natural History in Mayhoff’s section numbers. Traupman and Morgan–Owens do not have these words in the sections swept; they come from Lewis & Short.
